title: I’m thinking about an optional RTS difficulty where the AI gets smarter without cheating
author: DawnOfEmbers
selftext:
I’m Patrick, making Dawn of Embers, an RTS that’s still in development. One design question I keep coming back to is what “harder AI” should actually mean.



The opponent already makes some strategic choices: it picks a Calling and spends Discipline points before a match, scouts for map objectives called Pillars, and responds when its base is threatened. I’m considering whether a future, optional top difficulty could use a small language model to help it plan. That’s only an idea right now; it isn’t built, and the game currently has no AI service running during play.



I use AI tools in development too: some character bodies began in a generation tool and were then re-rigged, textured, and animated by hand; some concept and brand art, voices, sound effects, and music were AI-assisted; and I use coding assistants. I’m trying to be clear about that while keeping the game’s design and direction mine.



For people building AI-driven games: what would make a strategy opponent feel meaningfully smarter rather than just unfair? What would you want to see tested or explained before trusting an optional AI-planning difficulty?



I wrote more about the game and this idea in my latest dev update, if useful: [https://dawnofembers.com/updates/dev-update-02/](https://dawnofembers.com/updates/dev-update-02/)

comments.author: taisui
comments.body: You know, there are tons of veterans that worked on RTS games in the past 3 decades, if they could've done it they would have.  The point is not really have smart AI, the point is to provide challenge and entertaining AI.

replies.author: DawnOfEmbers
replies.body: I agree, my biggest thing with most AI's that I've come across in RTS games is it's a pretty static "AI Does this, do XYZ to counter" and once you figure out how it's going to play it's game, it's rinse and repeat. My thoughts around using true AI was to add some actual layer of thinking to it. Get it to learn and understand the game, the different playstyles, change it's tactics out of the standard scripted routes. May be a pipe dream in the end but it's at least where I'm hoping to take it towards but also looking for feedback to see if it's something people would even want to see in a game.

replies.author: egonosz
replies.body:
I want to warn you players do not really like smart game AI, they will assume it cheats or has some unfair advantage. 

And there is multiple way to implement game ai, you really do not need llm to make it good and fun. It depends on your target audience.

(I want to mention the webpage of the game and the game itself looks extremely AI generic .)

replies.author: DawnOfEmbers
replies.body: Fair feedback and appreciate it, am curious what specifically stood out to you? I'm so used to living in AI at this point between work and home projects with it so I tend to not notice these things as much.

replies.author: egonosz
replies.body: Well, that stood out to me you did not give Claude direction about visuals. Now imagine how I know you used Claude?

replies.author: FireDragon21976
replies.body: Sometimes in my designs I use the analogy of practical effects and stage magic - it's about creating the illusion of intelligence.   Players will appreciate those kinds of touches more than real raw intelligence, which is most cases just means getting stomped for the average player.

comments.author: lucianw
comments.body: I don't understand how the economics could ever add up. If your game makes an LLM call that costs 1c each time, and a user buys your game for $10, then after a few days of playing they've already used up $1 of your token allowance. A week and they've used up $2.

replies.author: DawnOfEmbers
replies.body: id be hosting a lightweight model on a VPS most likely, there would be cost associated still I agree, but it's cost I have other uses for so it would wash out in the end. I wouldn't be using a cloud token consumption approach because as you mention, it for sure wouldn't add up in the end.

comments.author: EtadanikM
comments.body:
LLM models are absolutely not the way to go for in-game strategic AI. It's like using a nuclear missile to cut a steak.

You have, honestly, *many* options for doing this. Frontier LLMs can created scripted AIs that utilize sophisticated algorithms to determine what to build, when to attack, etc. These can be highly competent, as the M28 AI in Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance shows. M28 was entirely scripted (by a human even), and plays at the level of high MMR players, so that should be your starting base line - tell Claude or Codex to download the M28 AI, break it down, and apply its techniques to your own game.

The alternative is to train a RL model. But this requires distributed compute that you probably don't have access to. Frontier LLMs can structure the RL curriculum but they cannot provide the compute, and if things go wrong or they get stuck in a loop, not knowing machine learning makes it hard to break them out of it. So not the best idea, but an option if you know what you're doing.

comments.author: Denaton_
comments.body: Its easy to make a difficult game, its hard to make a difficult game fun.

comments.author: PetiteGousseDAil
comments.body:
The smartest "AIs" in video game history are all just state machines

From what I have seen, the hard part is really more about making AIs *not* too strong, not the opposite

You really don't need an LLM to make an unbeatable AI

replies.author: FireDragon21976
replies.body: It depends on the game and the players.  A CPU opponent that's too weak may not be convincing in certain types of strategy games (look at the early Civ games, where it was obvious it was cheating).  But usually RTS games don't suffer from this because they have more in common with Doom than Stratego or Chess.

comments.author: FireDragon21976
comments.body: Don't use an LLM for planning.  Use Goal Oriented Action Planning for strategic planning, mixed with a behavior tree for individual units.

comments.author: orbital_trace
comments.body: For me, the AI should only get access to the same information the player int he same situiation would. It should also be limited to the number of moves its allowed to make per minute. After those two, you can optimize your ai agents to your hearts content.

comments.author: Smok3dSalmon
comments.body: Embers is a very popular AI title. Change the name. Nevermind you bought the URL already

comments.author: AxiosXiphos
comments.body: My own game has a seperate intelligence difficulty and stats difficulty. It's a nice way to give players more options.

comments.author: Crunchfest3
comments.body: A test I'd like to see: let it scout an undefended Pillar, then move defenders there after the scout leaves. Does it walk into the ambush, scout again, or somehow counter units it hasn't seen? An opponent that can be deceived would sell 'no cheating' to me better than an impressive win rate.
